# Dystonia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Movement disorders > Dystonia*

[Original Article Link](/library/A30ROf)

---

## Summary

Dystonia is a movement disorder characterized by sustained or intermittent muscle contractions causing involuntary movements, fixed postures, or both. The disorder may be <u>idiopathic</u>, hereditary, or acquired. Acquired dystonia is most commonly due to drugs (<u>antipsychotics</u>), metabolic disorders, <u>cerebrovascular disease</u>, or <u>traumatic brain injury</u>. Dystonia is classified according to the anatomic distribution of the symptoms into focal, multifocal, segmental, and generalized dystonia. Treatment involves pharmacologic management with <u>levodopa</u> or <u>anticholinergic agents</u>, as well as treatment of the underlying cause if possible. Focal dystonias respond well to periodic <u>botulinum toxin</u> injections in the affected muscle.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Idiopathic</u> (familial or sporadic)

* Hereditary (evidence of inherited genetic mutation)

* Acquired [[1]](/library/XMX9MA)

* Drugs: <u>dopamine antagonists</u>

* High-<u>potency</u> typical <u>antipsychotics</u> (e.g., <u>haloperidol</u>) are more likely than <u>atypical antipsychotics</u> to induce <u>acute dystonia</u>.

* <u>Metoclopramide</u>

* Neurologic disorders: <u>Huntington disease</u>

* Metabolic: <u>Wilson disease</u>

* <u>Hypoxic</u> or structural cerebral injury

* Cerebral <u>neoplasm</u>

* Infections: <u>encephalitis</u>, <u>HIV</u>

* Psychogenic: <u>conversion disorder</u>

* Toxic (e.g., cobalt)





> [!TIP]
> Most cases of <u>acute dystonia</u> are caused by <u>antipsychotic drugs</u>.

---

## Classification

Dystonia disorders are classified according to the distribution of symptoms in the body.




### Focal dystonia




* Affects a single region of the body

* The majority of cases are <u>idiopathic</u>.

* Onset typically in adulthood (usually > 30 years)

* Patients may have sensory tricks (geste antagonistes) with which they are able to suppress spasms (e.g., touching the affected region).





#### Conditions




* Spasmodic torticollis: <u>cervical dystonia</u> 

* Abnormal head movements  or fixed head posture

* Geste antagoniste: a voluntary maneuver that temporarily reduces the severity of dystonic postures or movements

* Blepharospasm: <u>eye dystonia</u>:  (e.g., increased blinking or involuntary <u>eye</u> closure); usually bilateral, symmetrical

* Spasmodic dysphonia: <u>laryngeal dystonia</u> or <u>voice dystonia</u>

* Voice breaks or strained voice (most common)  [[2]](/library/wQahy4)

* Weak, breathy voice

* Oromandibular dystonia: : involuntary movements of the <u>tongue</u>, <u>jaw</u>, and/or face (e.g., <u>jaw</u> clenching, <u>jaw</u> opening)

* Writer's dystonia (<u>writer's cramp</u>): non-painful contractions of hand muscles that are provoked by specific tasks (e.g., writing)





### Segmental dystonia




* Affects ≥ 2 adjacent regions of the body

* Meige syndrome: <u>blepharospasm</u> with <u>oromandibular dystonia</u>





### Generalized dystonia




* Affects the trunk and at least two additional regions of the body

* Typically early onset (< 21 years of age)





#### Conditions




* <u>Neuroleptic-induced acute dystonia</u>

* Dopa-responsive dystonia (<u>Segawa syndrome</u>): a rare, genetic disorder with onset in childhood (< 10 years; <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u>)

* Dystonia that responds well to treatment with <u>levodopa</u>

* <u>Parkinsonism</u>

* Torsion dystonia (<u>dystonia musculorum deformans</u>): a rare, <u>idiopathic</u> disorder with onset in childhood [[3]](/library/1va2_m)

* Initial focal dystonia: involuntary movements of the limbs, torso, and neck

* Progression to generalized dystonia





### Other types of dystonia [[4]](/library/cMXanA)




* Multifocal dystonia: affects ≥ 2 nonadjacent regions of the body

* Hemidystonia: affects the limbs of one half of the body

---

## Treatment

All treatments can be used for generalized dystonia, but <u>botulinum toxin</u> injections are typically reserved for focal dystonia. See “<u>Extrapyramidal syndrome</u>” for treatment of <u>acute dystonic reactions</u> due to <u>antipsychotics</u>. [[5]](/library/isaJuN)




* <u>Levodopa</u>/<u>carbidopa</u>: A trial should be taken in all patients with childhood-onset dystonia to distinguish dopa-responsive dystonia from the other forms.

* <u>Anticholinergics</u>:  (<u>benztropine</u>; , <u>trihexyphenidyl</u>) or <u>antihistamines</u> (<u>diphenhydramine</u>)  [[6]](/library/ksamEN)

* Periodic <u>botulinum toxin</u> injections: for focal dystonia  [[7]](/library/1MX2nA)

* <u>Deep brain stimulation</u>

* Treatment of underlying disorder of acquired dystonia:  (e.g., cessation of the causative drug)

* Supportive measures: <u>physiotherapy</u>, ergotherapy
